summary: LDAP is extensible: new operations, extended operations and schemas can be added. This document gives considerations for designers of LDAP extensions. It is a Best Current Practice document.

eli5.summary: Advice for people adding new features to the address-book system so their additions fit well.

questions: how to design an ldap extension
what is the ldap root dse
subtitle: Design advice for anyone adding new operations, schema or other features to LDAP.

tldr.problem: LDAP can be extended in many ways (new operations, new schema, new authentication methods), and careless extensions can break peers that do not know about them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives designers a checklist: keep extensions truly optional, use controls for complementary features and extended operations for new ones, provide discovery, register values, and follow rules for ASN.1 and schema.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 118) that standardizes how LDAP extensions are specified, without adding any protocol of its own.

today: RFC 4521 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 118), and the metadata for this RFC lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It leans on the LDAP core documents such as RFC 4510 and RFC 4511.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is an extensible protocol. It allows new operations to be added and existing ones enhanced, additional schema to be defined (object classes, attribute types, matching rules, syntaxes), and attribute types to be extended with options. It supports the extensible SASL authentication framework and Transport Layer Security (TLS), has an extensible URL format, and allows certain extensions to its ASN.1 definition.

This document describes practices that engineers should consider when designing extensions to LDAP. It uses the key words of BCP 14 (RFC 2119), applied to the engineering of LDAP extensions. A Request Control is attached to a client-generated message and a Response Control to a server-generated one.
sections.eli5: LDAP is built so people can add to it. This note gives advice for doing that well.

sections.title: General Considerations
sections.content:
Mutually agreeing peers may make significant changes to protocol semantics within an extension, but designers MUST consider the impact on peers that have not agreed to support it. Extensions MUST be truly optional. Designers SHOULD consider how their extension interacts with others and SHOULD make extensions themselves extensible.

Discovery. Extensions SHOULD provide adequate discovery. A client normally learns what a server supports by querying the root DSE. The supportedControl, supportedExtension and supportedFeatures attributes advertise controls, extended operations and features. LDAP has no way for a server to discover a client's capabilities.

Other rules. Extensions SHOULD NOT needlessly restrict applications to subsets of Unicode and SHOULD allow language tags on the attribute types they define. Extension elements described in ASN.1 and encoded with BER are RECOMMENDED to follow the restrictions of the core protocol's BER subset, so existing parsers can be reused. Examples SHOULD use the standard DN, filter, URL and LDIF formats. Protocol values SHALL be registered under BCP 64 (RFC 4520), and new extensible elements need registries under BCP 64 and BCP 26 (RFC 2434).
sections.eli5: New features must be optional, so old programs keep working. A program should be able to ask a server, "What extras do you have?" before using one.

sections.title: Extending Operations
sections.content:
Extensions SHOULD use controls for features that complement existing operations, and SHOULD consider an extended operation when the feature does not. The RFC's example: subtree delete complements delete, so a control suits it. A contrived locate-services operation, which returns LDAP URLs for services that may hold an entry, does not complement search, so it fits better as an extended operation.

Controls are the RECOMMENDED way to extend existing operations. Extensions SHOULD NOT return response controls unless the server knows the client can use them, and control specifications SHALL NOT attach extra meaning to criticality, though they MAY mandate a value such as TRUE or FALSE.

  • Bind and Start TLS: controls on these are not protected by the security layers they establish. The specification SHALL say so and say how the information is protected or why it need not be. Using an extended operation issued afterward is RECOMMENDED as an alternative.
  • Search: there are two phases, finding the base object and searching at or under it. The specification should say which phase(s) a control applies to.
  • Updates: specifications MUST say whether extra changes are in the same transaction as the base operation, and in what order changes are applied.
  • Abandon and Unbind: they have no response, so controls on them SHOULD be criticality FALSE.

An extended operation is an ExtendedRequest, zero or more IntermediateResponse messages and an ExtendedResponse. Extensions SHALL use IntermediateResponse, not ExtendedResponse, for intermediate results. Unsolicited notifications SHOULD NOT be sent unless the server knows the client can use them.
sections.eli5: If your new feature is a small tweak to something LDAP already does, attach it as a note to that request. If it is a brand new job, make it a new kind of request.

sections.title: Extending the ASN.1 Definition
sections.content:
LDAP allows limited extension of its ASN.1 definition. New result codes should give clients a clear indication of the outcome. Extensions SHOULD reuse existing codes where the meaning fits and MAY add new ones (registered per RFC 4520) when none does. They SHALL NOT restrict the return of general service result codes, especially those reporting protocol, service or security problems.

New LDAP message types are generally unnecessary and inappropriate. Extended operations, unsolicited notifications and intermediate responses SHOULD be used instead, and if none fits, a reusable new mechanism SHOULD be defined.

For authentication, Bind currently supports simple and SASL methods. New authentication processes are RECOMMENDED to be SASL mechanisms. No operation other than Bind SHALL be defined or extended to establish the LDAP association, though others MAY establish other security associations such as IPsec.

Because ASN.1 types are implicitly extensible, clients and servers MUST (unless otherwise specified) ignore trailing SEQUENCE components with unknown tags. Designers SHOULD avoid relying on this.
sections.eli5: Use the codes and message types that already exist when you can, and only add new ones when nothing fits. Never ask old programs to guess what mystery extras mean.

sections.title: Schema Extensions
sections.content:
Schema definitions SHALL use the syntax of the LDAP models document, and a reformatted (line wrapped) definition SHALL be noted. New elements SHOULD have one short NAME. The DESC field is informational only, so the specification MUST read the same with or without it. Published schema elements SHALL NOT be redefined; define replacements with new OIDs and NAMEs instead. Reuse is encouraged but MUST not alter semantics.

  • Syntaxes: each MUST specify its ASN.1 definition, and a distinct syntax SHOULD exist for each distinct definition. A string encoding SHOULD be defined, RECOMMENDED to be UTF-8, using GSER for complex types or a formal language such as ABNF. If none is defined, the extension SHALL say how the transfer encoding is indicated.
  • Matching rules: specify the kind (EQUALITY, ORDERING or SUBSTRING) and the values it applies to. Equality rules SHOULD be commutative.
  • Attribute types: servers only enforce the attribute's syntax, so an attribute meant for URIs but given a directoryString syntax is not limited to URIs. Matching rules MUST be compatible with the syntax. Operational attributes MUST say how servers maintain and use them.
  • Object classes: think carefully about which attributes are required (MUST) or allowed (MAY).
sections.eli5: When you add new kinds of address-book entries, give them clear short names, never change an old definition, and say exactly how the data is written down.

sections.title: Other Extension Mechanisms
sections.content: Three smaller mechanisms are covered briefly. Attribute description options are identified by a string of letters, numbers and hyphens that SHOULD be short. Authorization identities: extensions that use them SHALL support the LDAP authzId format, which is itself extensible. LDAP URL extensions are identified by a short descriptor string that SHOULD be short.
sections.eli5: Even the small add-ons, like labels and URL extras, should have short, simple names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: LDAP places no undue restrictions on extensions, and this document cannot cover every issue. Designers MUST do their own evaluation of the security considerations of their extensions. They MUST NOT assume that the LDAP core specification (RFC 4510) addresses the concerns specific to their extension, or that the extension has none. Specifications SHOULD note whether the security considerations of the feature being extended, and general LDAP ones, apply.
sections.eli5: Do your own safety check for your new feature. Do not assume someone else already did it.
